title: 真假金丝雀的博弈第8章
content_zh:
第8章 顾宅

    黑色奔驰停在别墅门口的时候，我看了眼手机。上午八点五十七分，比约定的九点早了整整三分钟。顾西辞说得对，不能给她准备时间。我不能让她有机会把这场谈话设计成另一个版本的茶会——安排好座位、台词和观众，然后等着我入瓮。今天没有观众。今天我也不会按照她的剧本来。

    老陈从驾驶座回过头来，脸上的表情有些复杂。他给我开了十八年的车门，从幼儿园到大学毕业，从顾家千金到落难假千金。今天早上顾西辞让他来接我的时候，他说他愣了一下才应声，因为“顾太太明明说的是让另一个司机去接温小姐，怎么变成了我”。

    “温小姐，”他把车停稳，犹豫了一下才开口，“太太今天早上一起来就在书房里坐着，窗帘都拉着。我看她脸色不太好，您注意点，别跟她硬碰。”

    “谢谢陈叔。我知道。”

    我推开车门下车。十一月的晨风凉得刺骨，别墅门前那两棵银杏树的叶子快落光了，在地上铺了厚厚一层金黄。门廊的柱子还是老样子，白色的罗马柱，左边第三根上面有一道划痕，是我十岁那年骑自行车撞的。当时我吓得大哭，怕被责骂，结果李婶帮我用牙膏涂了涂，说白色牙膏能遮白色划痕。后来那道划痕一直都在，只是没人注意过。除了我。

    我按了门铃。不是以前那个“回家”的节奏，是规规矩矩的短促一声。

    开门的是李婶。

    她看到我的一瞬间，手里的抹布掉在了地上。她的嘴唇哆嗦了两下，眼眶一下子就红了。但她没有出声，只是弯腰捡起抹布，侧身让我进门，然后用极低极快的声音在我耳边说了一句“厨房灶台上有一碗红豆汤，你爱喝的，趁热”。

    “李婶。”我叫了她一声。她摆摆手，转身快步走向厨房，围裙在走廊拐角处一闪就消失了。

    客厅还是老样子。黄花梨的家具，墙上挂着顾父收藏的字画，壁炉上的摆钟还在左右摇晃。空气里有百合花的香味，是从玄关那只花瓶里飘出来的。那只花瓶是我十五岁那年和顾母一起去挑的，当时我选了一只青花瓷的，她嫌太素，换成了现在的粉彩花鸟瓶。那大概是我为数不多的、母女之间像母女的时刻。

    顾母从楼梯上走下来。她穿了一件藏青色的旗袍，头发梳得一丝不苟，化了淡妆。三个月不见，她看起来瘦了一些，颧骨更突出了，但眼睛里的东西没变。那种审视的、评判的目光，从楼梯上投下来，像一束追光灯，把我从头扫到脚。

    “你来了。坐吧。”

    她指了指客厅的沙发。我注意到她没有叫我“温暖”，连“温小姐”都没有叫。她直接跳过了称呼，好像我们之间已经不存在任何可以被称谓概括的关系。

    我坐在沙发上。她坐在我对面的单人椅上，腰背挺得笔直，双手交叠放在膝盖上。这是她标准的会客姿态，不是对家人的，是对外人的。

    “你喝茶吗？”她问。

    “不用了。我不渴。”

    “你倒是不客气。”

    “您约我来，想必不是为了喝茶。”

    她的嘴角微微动了一下，不知道是笑意还是别的什么。客厅里很安静，只有壁炉上的摆钟在走动，每一下都像一根针扎在空气里。窗外有人经过——是园丁老周推着割草机走过草坪。我和老周隔着玻璃对视了一秒，他的表情像是见了鬼，割草机在草坪上停了一下才继续前进。

    “你在西辞那边，做得怎么样？”

    “正常。签了合同，按合同办事。”

    “按合同办事。”她把这几个字重复了一遍，语气里带着一丝难以捉摸的嘲讽，“你倒是学得快。以前在家的时候，你最讨厌看合同。西辞让你看一份两页的协议，你都说头疼。”

    “以前没有生存压力。”

    “现在有了？”

    “从您把行李放在后门的那一刻就有了。”

    她脸色变了。不是愤怒的变，是被戳中了某个痛处的变。她交叠在膝盖上的手指收紧了一下，指节微微泛白。

    “你以为把你送走是一件很容易的事吗？”

    “我没觉得容易。但您毕竟做了。”

    她站起来，走到玄关那只粉彩花鸟瓶旁边，背对着我。花瓶里的百合花开得正好，但她伸出手，捏住了一朵正在枯萎的。她把花瓣一片一片地扯下来，动作很慢，花瓣落在她脚边，像一片片碎掉的白纸。

    “那个消息，是我让人发的。”

    我整个人定在沙发上。想过很多种可能性。想过她不承认，想过她绕弯子，想过她用暗示的方式让我自己猜。但我没想过她会主动说出来。而且说得这么快。见面不到十分钟，椅子还没坐热，茶还没倒，她就直接掀了底牌。

    “为什么？”我问。

    “因为我想让你主动离开。”

    “您可以直接跟顾西辞说，让他跟我解约。为什么绕这么大一个圈子？”

    “你以为我没说？”她转过身来，手里的花茎已经被她掐断了，“三个月前，你从这扇门走出去的那天晚上，我就跟他说了。我说让她走，给她一笔钱，让她离开这座城市。他说不行。”

    “他为什么说不行？”

    “他没给我理由。他只是说不行。后来我又提了两次，最后一次他把茶杯砸在墙上，让我别再插手他的事。”她的声音在提到“砸茶杯”的时候终于失去了平稳，颤抖了一下，“他从小到大从来没有对我摔过东西。为了你。”

    我把这三个字含在嘴里，没有咽下去，也没有吐出来。顾西辞为他妈妈摔过茶杯。这件事他从来没有跟我提过。他只说她可能对你有意见，我来处理。他的处理方式是砸茶杯。

    “所以您就想逼我自己走。发恐吓消息，让我觉得这个城市不安全，让我觉得有人要我消失。”

    “对。”
content_en:
Chapter 8 Gu Zhai
When the black Mercedes-Benz parked at the door of the villa, I looked at my phone. It was 8:57 a.m., a full three minutes earlier than the agreed nine o'clock. Gu Xici was right, he couldn't give her time to prepare. I couldn't give her the chance to frame this conversation as another version of a tea party—arrange the seats, the lines, the audience, and then wait for me to die. There is no audience today. I won't follow her script today either.
Old Chen turned back from the driver's seat with a complicated expression on his face. He opened the door for me for eighteen years, from kindergarten to college graduation, from the daughter of the Gu family to the daughter of a family in distress. When Gu Xici asked him to pick me up this morning, he said he was stunned for a moment before he answered because "Mrs. Gu clearly said to ask another driver to pick up Miss Wen, why did it become me?"
"Ms. Wen," he stopped the car and hesitated before speaking, "My wife has been sitting in the study since she came up this morning, with the curtains closed. I think her face is not very good. Please be careful and don't confront her head-on."
"Thank you, Uncle Chen. I know."
I opened the door and got out of the car. The November morning breeze was bitingly cold, and the leaves of the two ginkgo trees in front of the villa were almost falling off, leaving a thick layer of golden color on the ground. The pillars of the porch are still the same, white Roman pillars. The third one from the left has a scratch on it. It was hit by my bicycle when I was ten years old. I was so frightened that I cried for fear of being scolded, so Aunt Li helped me apply toothpaste on it, saying that white toothpaste could cover the white scratches. The scratch was always there, but no one noticed it. Except me.
I rang the doorbell. It's not the "go home" rhythm before, it's a regular short sound.
It was Aunt Li who opened the door.
The moment she saw me, the rag in her hand fell to the ground. Her lips trembled twice, and her eyes suddenly turned red. But she didn't say anything. She just bent down to pick up the rag, turned aside to let me in, and then said in my ear in a very low and fast voice, "There is a bowl of red bean soup on the kitchen stove. If you like it, keep it warm."
"Aunt Li." I called her. She waved her hands, turned around and walked quickly to the kitchen, her apron disappearing in a flash around the corner of the corridor.
The living room is still the same. Huanghuali furniture, calligraphy and paintings collected by Gu's father are hung on the wall, and the pendulum clock on the fireplace is still swinging from side to side. There is the fragrance of lilies in the air, coming from the vase in the entrance hall. That vase was picked out by my mother and I when I was fifteen years old. I chose a blue and white porcelain one, but she thought it was too plain, so she replaced it with the current pastel flower and bird vase. That was probably one of the few moments where mother and daughter were like mother and daughter.
Gu's mother came down the stairs. She wore a navy blue cheongsam, her hair was combed meticulously, and she put on light makeup. After not seeing her for three months, she seemed to have lost some weight and her cheekbones were more prominent, but the things in her eyes remained the same. That scrutinizing, judgmental gaze cast down from the stairs, like a spotlight, sweeping me from head to toe.
"You're here. Sit down."
She pointed to the sofa in the living room. I noticed that she didn't call me "Nuan Nuan", not even "Miss Wen". She skipped the title, as if there was no relationship between us that could be summed up by the title.
I'm sitting on the couch. She sat on the single chair opposite me, with her back straight and her hands folded on her knees. This is her standard greeting gesture, not to family members, but to outsiders.
"Do you have tea?" she asked.
"No need. I'm not thirsty."
"You're welcome."
"You probably didn't invite me here for tea."
The corners of her mouth moved slightly, not sure if it was a smile or something else. The living room was very quiet, except for the pendulum clock on the fireplace moving, and every tick was like a needle pricking the air. Someone passed by outside the window - it was Lao Zhou, the gardener, pushing a lawn mower across the lawn. Lao Zhou and I looked at each other for a second through the glass. His expression looked like he had seen a ghost. The lawnmower stopped on the lawn for a moment before moving on.
"How are you doing in Xici?"
"It's normal. I signed the contract and acted according to the contract."
"According to the contract." She repeated these words with a hint of elusive sarcasm in her tone. "You learn quickly. When you were at home, you hated reading contracts. When west Ci asked you to read a two-page agreement, you said you had a headache."
"There was no pressure to survive before."
"Now?"
“It’s there from the moment you put your luggage at the back door.”
Her expression changed. It's not a change of anger, it's a change of being poked at a certain sore spot. Her fingers folded on her knees tightened, and her knuckles turned slightly white.
"Did you think it would be easy to send you away?"
"I didn't find it easy. But you did it after all."
She stood up and walked to the pastel flower and bird vase in the entrance hall, with her back to me. The lilies in the vase were in bloom, but she stretched out her hand and pinched one that was withering. She pulled off the petals one by one, very slowly, and the petals fell at her feet, like pieces of broken white paper.
"That news was sent by me."
I froze on the sofa. I thought about many possibilities. I thought about her not admitting it, thought about her going around the bush, thought about her using hints to make me guess. But I never thought she would take the initiative to say it. And said so quickly. Less than ten minutes after meeting, before the chair was warm and before the tea was poured, she revealed her trump card.
"Why?" I asked.
"Because I want you to leave on your own initiative."
"You can tell Gu Xici directly and ask him to terminate the contract with me. Why go around in such a big circle?"
"You think I didn't tell you?" She turned around, the flower stem in her hand had been cut off, "I told him three months ago, the night you walked out of this door. I told her to let her go, give her a sum of money, and let her leave the city. He said no."
"Why did he say no?"
"He didn't give me a reason. He just said no. Then I mentioned it twice more. The last time he smashed the tea cup against the wall and told me not to interfere with his affairs." Her voice finally lost its balance when she mentioned "smashing the tea cup" and trembled. "He has never thrown anything at me since he was a child. For you."
I held these three words in my mouth without swallowing or spitting them out. Gu Xici threw the tea cup for his mother. He never mentioned this to me. He only said that she might have a problem with you and I would handle it. His way of dealing with it was to smash the tea cup.
"So you just want to force me to leave on my own. Send threatening messages to make me feel that this city is unsafe and that someone wants me to disappear."
"right."
title_en: The Game of True and False Canaries Chapter 8
